lead: Roads, railways and canals change direction and gradient through curves. A simple circular curve joins two straights with an arc of one radius. A transition curve placed between a straight and the arc lets the curvature, and the superelevation that balances it, grow gradually instead of jumping. A vertical curve, usually a parabola, joins two gradients at a summit or a valley. Each is computed, then pegged at regular chainages.
prereq: You need: horizontal angles from Measurement of horizontal and vertical angles, chainage along a line, and reduced levels from levelling.

sections.h3: Simple circular curve: elements and chainages

blocks.text: Two straights meet at the point of intersection I; the deflection angle Δ is the angle through which the forward straight turns from the back straight. An arc of radius R touches the back straight at the first tangent point T₁ and the forward straight at T₂. The degree of curve D is the angle at the centre subtended by a 30 m arc, so R = 1718.9 ÷ D (D in degrees).

Tangent length T = R tan(Δ/2);   length of curve l = πRΔ ÷ 180
Long chord = 2R sin(Δ/2);   apex (external) distance E = R[sec(Δ/2) − 1];   mid-ordinate M = R[1 − cos(Δ/2)]
Chainage of T₁ = chainage of I − T;   chainage of T₂ = chainage of T₁ + l
blocks.where: R in m, Δ in degrees. T is measured along each straight from I to the tangent point. E is from I to the middle of the curve, and M from the middle of the long chord to the curve. The chainage of T₂ is reached along the curve, so it is found by adding l to T₁, not T to I.

blocks.text: Pegs go at full chainages (every 20 m or 30 m), with a sub-chord at each end. The methods are:

items: Linear methods (tape only, for short curves): offsets from the long chord, y = √(R² − x²) − (R − M) with x from the midpoint of the chord; or offsets from the tangent, y = R − √(R² − x²), about x² ÷ (2R) for small x, with x measured along the tangent from T₁.

Rankine's method of tangential angles (theodolite and tape): set the theodolite at T₁ on 0°00′00″ towards I. For a chord c the tangential angle is δ = 1718.9 c ÷ R minutes. Turn the total deflection (the running sum of δ) and measure the chord from the previous peg to cut the line of sight. The total deflection to T₂ must equal Δ/2.

Two-theodolite method (no taping, rough ground): instruments at T₁ and T₂ turn the total deflections and the two lines of sight cross at each peg. A total station sets out each peg from its computed coordinates.

blocks.text: Entering a circular curve straight from a tangent, a vehicle would meet the full radial acceleration V² ÷ R and superelevation at once. A transition curve is a spiral whose radius falls from infinity at the tangent to R at the circular arc, so that the radial acceleration grows at a steady rate. For the ideal (clothoid) spiral the radius r at distance l along it satisfies r l = R Ls; for setting out, its offsets from the tangent are close to the cubic parabola y = x³ ÷ (6 R Ls).

Length by rate of change of radial acceleration:  L<sub>s</sub> = V³ ÷ (c R)
Shift S = L<sub>s</sub>² ÷ (24 R);   total tangent length = (R + S) tan(Δ/2) + L<sub>s</sub> ÷ 2;   equilibrium superelevation e = V² ÷ (g R)
blocks.where: V is the design speed in m/s, c the permitted rate of change of radial acceleration in m/s³ (about 0.3 to 0.6), R the radius in m, L<sub>s</sub> the transition length in m. The shift S moves the circular arc in to make room for the transitions. e is a ratio (rise per unit width); codes cap it, and tyre friction carries the rest.

blocks.text: Two gradients g₁ and g₂ (as decimals, + rising, − falling in the direction of chainage) meet at the vertical point of intersection. A summit curve has g₂ < g₁; a valley (sag) curve has g₂ > g₁. A parabola gives a constant rate of change of gradient, and its offsets from the tangent are simple to compute.
Length L<sub>v</sub> = (g₂ − g₁) ÷ r;   level on the curve at distance x from its start = tangent level + (g₂ − g₁) x² ÷ (2 L<sub>v</sub>)
blocks.where: r is the permitted rate of change of gradient per metre (sight distance may govern instead). Tangent level = start level + g₁ x. On a summit (g₂ − g₁) is negative and the curve lies below the tangent. The highest or lowest point is at x = −g₁ L<sub>v</sub> ÷ (g₂ − g₁).

examples.question: Two straights meet at I, chainage 2450.000 m, with a deflection angle of 40°. They are joined by a circular curve of radius 300 m, to be set out by Rankine's method with pegs at every 20 m of chainage. (a) Find the tangent length, curve length, long chord, apex distance and mid-ordinate. (b) Find the chainages of T₁ and T₂. (c) Tabulate the tangential angles and total deflections. (d) Find the length of transition for 80 km/h with c = 0.3 m/s³, and the shift.
steps: (c) First sub-chord to chainage 2360: c₁ = 2360 − 2340.81 = 19.19 m. Then nine full chords of 20 m reach 2540, and the last sub-chord is 2550.25 − 2540 = 10.25 m.
Check: the total deflection to T₂ equals Δ/2 = 20°00′00″.
examples.answer: T = 109.19 m, l = 209.44 m, long chord 205.21 m, E = 19.25 m, M = 18.09 m. T₁ at 2340.81 m and T₂ at 2550.25 m; total deflections from 1°49′57″ at 2360 to 20°00′00″ at T₂. Transition 121.9 m (125 m adopted) with a shift of 2.17 m.

examples.question: A rising gradient of +2.0 % meets a falling gradient of −1.5 % at chainage 1500 m, RL 105.000 m. A summit curve 200 m long is used. Find the RLs on the curve at 50 m intervals and the highest point.
steps: x = 50: tangent 104.000, correction −0.219, curve RL 103.781 m. x = 100: tangent 105.000, correction −0.875, RL 104.125 m.
examples.answer: Curve RLs 103.000, 103.781, 104.125, 104.031 and 103.500 m at chainages 1400 to 1600 m; summit at chainage 1514.29 m, RL 104.143 m.

traps: Finding T₂ as chainage of I + T. The route goes round the curve, so T₂ = T₁ + l.
Reversing the transition rule. L<sub>s</sub> = V³ ÷ (c R): a sharper curve (smaller R) needs a longer transition.
Dropping the sign of (g₂ − g₁). On a summit it is negative and the curve lies below the tangents.

quiz.q: Define the degree of a curve and give its relation to the radius for a 30 m arc.
quiz.a: The angle at the centre subtended by a 30 m arc (or chord). R = 1718.9 ÷ D, with D in degrees.

quiz.q: Why is a transition curve needed between a straight and a circular curve?
quiz.a: Otherwise V² ÷ R and the superelevation jump from zero at the tangent point; the transition applies both gradually, with no jerk.

quiz.q: A circular curve has R = 250 m and Δ = 50°. Find the tangent length and the curve length.
Find the transition length for 60 km/h, R = 200 m and c = 0.4 m/s³.
For R = 150 m, the offset from the tangent at 50 m is 8.58 m by y = R − √(R² − x²) but 8.33 m by x² ÷ (2R). When is the approximation acceptable?
quiz.a: The difference grows roughly as x⁴ ÷ (8R³): 0.25 m here, at x/R = 1/3. For short offsets (x under about a tenth of R, where it is a few millimetres) the parabola is fine; for long ones on a sharp curve the exact formula must be used.

quiz.q: On rough, rocky ground, would you set out a curve by Rankine's method or by two theodolites? Justify.
quiz.a: Two theodolites. Rankine's method needs every chord taped from peg to peg, which is slow and error-prone over rocks; with instruments at T₁ and T₂ each peg is fixed by the crossing of two lines of sight and needs no taping.

beyond: Not for the exam. Design software builds alignments from straights, clothoids and arcs and computes every peg's coordinates for total station or GNSS stakeout. Vertical curves are often specified by a K value tied to sight distance. Search for clothoid alignment design, K value vertical curve and stakeout with total station.
